Thanks for the note, Jordan — good questions. I'll summarize how Redwood counts "active context" for billing and include a couple of examples so you can map to your traffic patterns. TL;DR: active context is a per-conversation billing allocation that captures the longest contiguous prompt + history kept for KV reuse during the billing window; we bucket and floor before tokenization credits are applied.

Principles (short):
- Active context window: we treat a conversation as the same context while there's less than a 30-minute inactivity gap (TTL configurable per-customer; for most hosted customers default = 30m). If no request occurs for >30m, we close that context for billing purposes and a subsequent message starts a new active context.
- Token accounting: for each active context we take the maximum observed context length (in tokens) during the billing period and bill on that maximum. This prevents double-counting short reuses but ensures long histories are accounted for.
- Bucketing / rounding: to make billing stable we round each measured max-context up to the nearest 128-token bucket and then apply a per-context minimum floor of 512 tokens (i.e., minimum billable context = 512 tokens).
- Microbursts / short sessions: sessions that last less than 10s or with a single request producing <64 tokens are eligible for microburst crediting and are not escalated to the minimum 512 token floor; instead they are billed at actual token usage (rounded to nearest 64 tokens).

Example A — single user long chat:
- User opens chat at 09:00 and exchanges messages leading to a largest context of 3,410 tokens during March billing window.
- We round 3,410 up to 3,520 (nearest 128) => bill 3,520 tokens for that active context.

Example B — multiple short bursts within 20 minutes:
- Same user sends two short prompts at 10:05 and 10:18 (13 mins apart). Context TTL = 30m so we consider this one active context. Max context length observed = 180 tokens.
- Round up to nearest 128 => 256 tokens, apply floor 512 => bill 512 tokens for that active context.

Why we pick this approach:
- Bucketing reduces invoice volatility when you have many slightly different context lengths across sessions.
- Max-per-window avoids double-counting repeated accesses to the same long history in the same billing period.
- Microburst path prevents punishing customers for transient quick queries.

Adding the numeric walk-through so Acme can map to Feb usage. Markus covered the rules; here's quick math with the Feb numbers Jordan attached.

Assumptions from their invoice sample:
- 12,400 billed active-context tokens (across 2,300 active contexts) reported on invoice line.
- Our raw token counts from logs: sum(actual max context per conversation) = 10,860 tokens.

How the difference arises (illustrative):
- Rounding to 128 buckets increases 10,860 -> 11,264 (round each context up before summing).
- Applying 512-floor for the 1,200 small-context conversations (those with max <512) adds floor for each: those 1,200 become 1,200 * 512 = 614,400 billed tokens; raw for those = ~300,000 tokens. The floor explains the bulk of the gap.

Negotiation point (suggested):
- For committed deals we can map discount tiers to "monthly committed active-contexts" rather than raw tokens. E.g., ACME-2417: commit 50k active-contexts/month (counts by active conversation, not tokens) and provide a blended discount that smooths the impact of the 512 floor. This works well for customers whose pattern is many small chats.

Proposal for ACME-2417:
- If Acme commits to 50k active-contexts/month we can cap the effective per-context floor to 256 tokens for those committed units and apply a 7% volume discount on overage tokens.
- We can also offer a pilot concession for the first 2 months to remeasure TTL sensitivity.

Markus / Vanessa: want me to draft the amendment language for that concession? Jordan — if that structure sounds reasonable we can send a redline.
